Physics · Mechanics & Energy

Trail Physics

The physics of riding itself. How a rider speeds up, flies off a jump, grips through a corner and stops, and how the bike’s wheels, brakes and suspension do their jobs.

6 units · 17 modules · 3 learning activities

Units

  1. Unit 1 Physics Foundations 3 modules · 2 with activities

    What physics is, the maths it runs on, and how to measure the world honestly.

    1. Module 1

      Introduction to Physics

      What physics studies, how scientists build models and laws, and why a mountain bike is a physical system.

      • Describe what physics studies, with examples from riding
      • Tell an observation, a model, a law and a theory apart
      • Describe a mountain bike as a physical system of interacting parts
      • Name the physics each part of a bike depends on
      Activities in development Lesson coming

    2. Module 2

      Mathematics Review

      The algebra, ratios, geometry and trigonometry that every later module uses, practised on riding problems.

      • Rearrange an equation to solve for any of its variables
      • Use ratios and proportions in riding problems
      • Find a missing side of a right triangle
      • Use sine, cosine and tangent to find sides and angles
      • Calculate a trail’s grade from elevation change and horizontal distance
      • Read and interpret a graph of a riding quantity
      1 activity Lesson coming

    3. Module 3

      Scientific Measurement

      SI units, conversions, scientific notation, significant figures and uncertainty: how to collect data and say how sure you are.

      • Use SI base and derived units
      • Convert between units, such as km/h, m/s and mph
      • Write and calculate with scientific notation
      • Report a result with sensible significant figures
      • Estimate a measurement’s uncertainty and percent uncertainty
      • Name a model’s assumptions and when they stop holding
      1 activity Lesson coming
  2. Unit 2 Understanding Motion 3 modules · 1 with activities

    Describe motion in one and two dimensions, from a rider on a straight trail to a rider in the air.

    1. Module 4

      Motion in One Dimension

      Position, displacement, velocity and acceleration, and the graphs and equations that describe a rider on a straight trail.

      • Tell distance from displacement, and speed from velocity
      • Calculate average velocity from a change in position
      • Calculate acceleration, including braking
      • Use the constant-acceleration equations to predict position and speed
      • Read and sketch position-, velocity- and acceleration-time graphs
      • Describe free fall, with g ≈ 9.8 m/s²
      Activities in development Lesson coming

    2. Module 5

      Vectors

      Quantities with a size and a direction: how to add them, split them into components and find a resultant.

      • Tell scalar and vector quantities apart
      • Add and subtract vectors, by drawing and by components
      • Resolve a vector into horizontal and vertical components
      • Find a resultant’s magnitude and direction
      Activities in development Lesson coming

    3. Module 6

      Projectile Motion

      Motion in two dimensions: why horizontal and vertical motion are independent, and how to predict flight time, height and range.

      • Split a takeoff velocity into horizontal and vertical components
      • Explain why horizontal and vertical motion are independent
      • Calculate flight time, maximum height and horizontal range
      • Predict where a rider lands, using the trajectory equations
      • Explain how takeoff speed and angle change a trajectory
      1 activity Lesson coming
  3. Unit 3 Forces & Cornering 3 modules · 2 with activities

    Newton’s laws, friction and springs, and the physics of turning.

    1. Module 7

      Newton’s Laws of Motion

      Force, mass and inertia; Newton’s three laws; net force and free-body diagrams.

      • Explain inertia and Newton’s first law
      • Combine forces to find the net force
      • Use F_net = ma to find a force, mass or acceleration
      • Identify action-reaction pairs, such as tire and trail
      • Draw a free-body diagram for a rider and bike
      Activities in development Lesson coming

    2. Module 8

      Friction, Slopes and Springs

      Newton’s laws at work: the normal force, static and kinetic friction, inclined planes, Hooke’s law and how materials deform.

      • Find the normal force, on flat ground and on a slope
      • Use the friction model F_f = μN for static and kinetic friction
      • Split gravity into parts along and across a slope
      • Use Hooke’s law for a spring
      • Describe elastic deformation, stress and strain
      1 activity Lesson coming

    3. Module 9

      Uniform Circular Motion

      Turning: arc length, angular velocity, centripetal acceleration and force, and how a banked turn helps.

      • Relate arc length, angle and radius
      • Relate angular velocity, speed and radius with ω = v/r
      • Calculate centripetal acceleration with a = v²/r
      • Calculate the inward force a turn needs and identify what supplies it
      • Explain how speed and radius change the demands of a corner
      • Explain how a banked turn supplies inward force, and find the matched bank angle
      1 activity Lesson coming
  4. Unit 4 Energy & Momentum 3 modules

    Energy, work, power and momentum: the bookkeeping of a ride.

    1. Module 10

      Energy and Gravitation

      Kinetic, gravitational and elastic potential energy, conservation of mechanical energy, and Newton’s law of gravitation.

      • Calculate kinetic energy
      • Calculate gravitational potential energy
      • Use conservation of mechanical energy to predict speed after a descent
      • Calculate the energy stored in a compressed spring
      • Account for energy lost to friction and other non-conservative forces
      • Describe Newton’s law of gravitation and gravitational fields
      Activities in development Lesson coming

    2. Module 11

      Work and Power

      Work, the work-energy theorem, power and efficiency: what it costs to ride a trail.

      • Calculate the work done by a force
      • Use the work-energy theorem
      • Calculate average power, including climbing power
      • Compare riders using power-to-weight ratio
      • Calculate and interpret energy efficiency
      Activities in development Lesson coming

    3. Module 12

      Momentum and Collisions

      Momentum, impulse and conservation of momentum, and why stretching out a collision lowers the average force.

      • Calculate momentum
      • Use the impulse-momentum theorem
      • Explain why a longer interaction time means a smaller average force
      • Use conservation of momentum in a collision
      • Tell elastic and inelastic collisions apart
      Activities in development Lesson coming
  5. Unit 5 Bike Mechanics 3 modules · 1 with activities

    The engineering of the bike: drivetrains and wheels, hydraulic brakes, and suspension.

    1. Module 13

      Rotational Dynamics

      Angular velocity and acceleration, torque, moment of inertia, gear ratios and rotational energy.

      • Relate angular velocity, linear speed and radius
      • Calculate a gear ratio and explain mechanical advantage
      • Follow rotation from crank to wheel to find distance and speed
      • Calculate torque from a force and a lever arm
      • Explain moment of inertia and why wheel mass matters
      • Calculate rotational kinetic energy
      1 activity Lesson coming

    2. Module 14

      Fluids

      Density, pressure, Pascal’s principle and hydraulics, buoyancy, flow and air resistance.

      • Calculate density from mass and volume
      • Calculate pressure from force and area
      • Use Pascal’s principle to explain a hydraulic brake
      • Calculate the force multiplication between pistons of different areas
      • Use the continuity equation for steady flow
      • Describe Bernoulli’s principle and air resistance
      Activities in development Lesson coming

    3. Module 15

      Oscillations

      Restoring forces, simple harmonic motion, period and frequency, energy in a spring, and damping.

      • Describe a restoring force with Hooke’s law
      • Calculate the period and frequency of a spring-mass system
      • Read displacement, velocity and acceleration graphs of simple harmonic motion
      • Track spring and kinetic energy through an oscillation
      • Describe how damping changes an oscillation
      Activities in development Lesson coming
  6. Unit 6 Waves & Temperature 2 modules

    Vibrations, sound and waves, then heat, temperature and the laws of thermodynamics.

    1. Module 16

      Waves

      Wave motion, wavelength, frequency and speed, superposition and interference, sound and resonance.

      • Identify wavelength, frequency, amplitude and period
      • Use v = fλ and T = 1/f
      • Tell transverse and longitudinal waves apart
      • Predict constructive and destructive interference
      • Describe sound as a wave, and resonance
      Activities in development Lesson coming

    2. Module 17

      Thermodynamics

      Temperature, heat and thermal energy, heat transfer, the ideal gas law and the first and second laws.

      • Tell temperature, heat and thermal energy apart, and convert temperature scales
      • Use Q = mcΔT
      • Estimate a brake’s temperature rise from kinetic energy, stating the assumptions
      • Use the ideal gas law for a tire
      • Apply the first law of thermodynamics with a stated sign convention
      • Explain the second law and why no engine is 100% efficient
      Activities in development Lesson coming
